summary: The Gemara establishes: halacha follows R. Yosei - the replacement KG cannot serve in either capacity while the original lives. If the original dies, the replacement returns fully. Rav needs to state this lest you think the replacement is like a tzarah whose disqualified status, once attached during the other's lifetime, persists even after the other dies. The discussion then turns to R. Yehuda's view that the sages should also prepare a backup wife, not just a backup KG. The Rabbanan initially distinguish the risks by frequency: impurity is shechicha (common), while a wife's death is lo shechicha (not common). The Gemara then tests both sides with a no-end slippery slope: R. Yehuda distinguishes concern for one death from concern for two, while the Rabbanan defend preparing a backup priest because appointing a rival makes the Kohen Gadol still more diligent. The rest of the page explores four conditional-divorce formulas for the backup wife under the Torah's requirement of a single bayit (household), ending unresolved at the boundary with 13b.

display.title: No lingering disqualification: the replacement KG resumes cleanly when the original dies
display.oneLine: Rav rules that the replacement KG returns to full status the moment the original dies, rejecting the tzarat ervah analogy that might suggest the disqualification persists.
display.whats: The Gemara rules: halacha follows R. Yosei. The replacement KG is suspended from both offices while the original lives. Critically, R. Yosei agrees that if the replacement violated this and served anyway, his service is valid. Rav Yehuda adds: if the original dies, the replacement resumes full KG status. The Gemara asks - isn't that obvious? The answer: Rav must state it lest you think the replacement's disqualification persists by analogy to tzarat ervah - a status attaching during another's lifetime that can remain in force even after that other party dies.
display.hint: The tzarah analogy is technical, not emotional: in the law of tzarat ervah, a status that attaches to a party during another's lifetime can persist even after that other party dies - the tzarah must 'wait for the other to die,' and her permitted status is not automatic even then. So why doesn't the replacement KG's disqualification - which likewise attached during the original's lifetime, due to professional rivalry (kinah) over holding the office - persist the same way once the original dies?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does Rav need to state that the replacement KG resumes full status when the original dies, if that seems obvious?
learning.coreTension: The replacement's disqualification attached during the original's lifetime, so it might seem to persist by analogy to tzarat ervah - where a status attaching during another's lifetime can remain in force even after that other party dies - even though it is really just a contingent legal status tied to the original's life.
learning.coreMove: Rav rules that the replacement-original relationship is not like a tzarah whose enmity outlasts the rival; it is a clean legal contingency that dissolves the moment the original dies, so the replacement resumes fully without restriction.
learning.ahaMoment: A disqualification's persistence depends on its own legal mechanics, not merely on when it attached: the replacement's disqualification was contingent on the original's life, so it dissolves at death, unlike a tzarah's status under tzarat ervah which can persist past the other party's death.
learning.memoryAnchor: Not governed by tzarat ervah persistence - the KG-replacement's disqualification dissolves cleanly when the original dies, unlike a tzarah of an ervah, whose status can remain even after the other party's death.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may wonder why the tzarah analogy is raised at all, since the replacement KG and the original are not wives to each other. The point is technical: the Gemara is testing whether the rule that a status attaching during another's lifetime can outlast that other's death (as with tzarat ervah) extends by analogy to this disqualification. Rav rejects the analogy, not an interpersonal-enmity reading that was never the actual concern.

takeaway.text: Halacha follows R. Yosei: the replacement KG is suspended from both offices while the original lives, and resumes full status the moment the original dies, with no lingering tzarah-like enmity.

argumentFlow.label: Halacha: R. Yosei
argumentFlow.speaker: Anonymous Gemara / Rav Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: Halacha follows R. Yosei: the replacement KG cannot serve as KG or common priest while the original lives. If he served anyway, his service is valid. If the original dies, the replacement resumes full KG status.

sourceRefs.note: Core ruling

argumentFlow.label: Is the 'return to service' ruling obvious?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks: isn't it obvious that the replacement returns after the original dies? Why does Rav need to state this?

sourceRefs.note: Challenge to Rav's statement

argumentFlow.label: Lest you think: tzarah - permanent rivalry
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav must state this because you might think the replacement's disqualification persists by analogy to tzarat ervah - where a status attaching during another's lifetime can remain in force even after that other party's death. Rav teaches that this analogy does not apply here - the replacement resumes cleanly the moment the original dies.

misconceptions.misconception: The replacement's service is invalid if he served while suspended.
misconceptions.correction: R. Yosei explicitly concedes the service is valid even though the replacement violated the suspension.

misconceptions.misconception: The tzarah analogy means the replacement KG and original share some kind of personal rivalry or enmity that could outlast the original's death.
misconceptions.correction: The tzarah analogy invokes the technical law of tzarat ervah - a disqualified status attaching during another's lifetime that can persist after that party's death - not interpersonal enmity. Rav teaches that this specific disqualification does not persist by that analogy; it lapses cleanly when the original dies.

display.title: Backup wife or just backup priest? Frequency decides - then two reciprocal challenges
display.oneLine: R. Yehuda wants a backup wife prepared like the backup KG; the Rabbanan answer on frequency alone (shechicha vs. lo shechicha), then both sides trade slippery-slope challenges - one about multiple deaths, one about the Rabbanan's own backup-KG rule.
display.whats: R. Yehuda holds that the sages should prepare not only a replacement KG (in case of impurity) but also a replacement wife (in case his wife dies before Yom Kippur, since the Torah says 'his house' - he must have a wife on YK). The Rabbanan disagree on frequency alone: impurity before Yom Kippur is shechicha (a common occurrence), so preparing a backup KG is warranted; the wife's death before Yom Kippur is lo shechicha (not a common occurrence), so no backup wife is needed. The Gemara then presses R. Yehuda with a slippery-slope challenge: if any risk of death to a wife matters, there is no end to the matter - what about a second wife dying too? R. Yehuda answers that he is only concerned about one death, not a run of two; the Rabbanan reply that if they are concerned at all, they would be concerned even for two. Finally the Gemara turns the same kind of challenge back on the Rabbanan themselves: if the KG is diligent enough to avoid impurity on his own, why prepare a backup KG at all? The Rabbanan answer that it is precisely because a rival KG has been prepared that he is spurred to be extra vigilant.
display.hint: Why must these three moves stay distinct: the Rabbanan's frequency distinction (impurity is shechicha, death is lo shechicha), R. Yehuda's one-death-versus-two-deaths limit, and the later claim that appointing a rival backup priest makes the Kohen Gadol more diligent?

learning.learnerQuestion: If the sages prepare a backup KG against the risk of impurity, why don't they also prepare a backup wife - and once the Gemara starts worrying about rare risks, why does it stop at one extra death, and why prepare a backup KG if he's already expected to be careful?
learning.coreTension: R. Yehuda's logical symmetry, prepare for both risks alike, collides with the Rabbanan's view that preparation only makes sense for a risk that actually occurs with some frequency - and once that symmetry argument is raised, it threatens to run away in both directions (how many deaths? how much diligence?).
learning.coreMove: The Rabbanan first distinguish a common risk from a rare one: impurity before Yom Kippur is shechicha (common), so a backup KG is warranted; the wife's death before Yom Kippur is lo shechicha (not common), so no backup wife is warranted. The Gemara then challenges R. Yehuda that this logic has no natural stopping point (why worry about one death and not two?); R. Yehuda limits his concern to a single death, but the Rabbanan note that real concern should not stop at one. Finally the Gemara flips the same challenge onto the Rabbanan's own rule and they answer that preparing a rival KG is itself what makes the sitting KG diligent.
learning.ahaMoment: Preparation tracks likelihood, not just possibility - but likelihood-based lines invite 'where do you stop?' challenges on both sides. R. Yehuda draws his own stopping point (one death, not a cascade); the Rabbanan draw theirs by explaining that the backup KG isn't redundant with the sitting KG's diligence - it's the cause of it.
learning.memoryAnchor: Tumah shechicha, mitah lo shechicha (impurity is common, death is not common) is the opening distinction; 'ein ladavar sof' (there is no end to the matter) is the slippery-slope challenge that follows; 'kol shekein demizdarez tfei' (all the more diligent) is the Rabbanan's diligence defense that follows that.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may fold the diligence defense into the opening distinction, as if the Rabbanan originally justified preparing a backup KG by appeal to diligence. They did not - the opening distinction is purely about frequency (shechicha vs. lo shechicha). Diligence only enters later, as the Rabbanan's answer to a separate challenge: why prepare a backup KG at all if he's expected to be careful on his own?

takeaway.text: Preparation is warranted only where the risk is common (shechicha) - that is the Rabbanan's original, frequency-only reason for a backup KG but not a backup wife. A later, separate challenge asks why bother with a backup KG if the KG is diligent; the Rabbanan's answer is that the presence of a rival KG is what makes him diligent in the first place, not a reason to skip the preparation.

argumentFlow.label: R. Yehuda: prepare a backup wife too
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: Just as the sages prepare a replacement KG in case of impurity, they should also prepare a replacement wife in case his wife dies before Yom Kippur - since 'his house' (bayto) requires him to have a wife on the day.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yehuda's position

argumentFlow.label: Rabbanan: death is not like impurity - frequency, not conceptual preventability
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbanan
argumentFlow.text: The KG's wife dying before Yom Kippur and him becoming impure are not alike: impurity is shechicha (a common occurrence), so it is worth preparing for. Death is lo shechicha (not a common occurrence), so no backup wife is needed. This is a frequency distinction only, not yet any claim about diligence.

sourceRefs.note: Rabbanan's frequency distinction - tumah shechicha, mitah lo shechicha

argumentFlow.label: If so, there's no end to the matter - what about a second death?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara presses R. Yehuda: if even a rare risk of death justifies preparing a backup wife, there is no natural stopping point - why not also prepare for a second wife dying, and a third? R. Yehuda answers that he is only concerned about a single death, not a run of two deaths. The Rabbanan counter that this limit is arbitrary: if one is concerned at all, one should be concerned even for two deaths.

sourceRefs.note: The no-end challenge begins
R. Yehuda: concern for one death, not two
The reciprocal challenge is turned toward the Rabbanan
If concern applies at all, why not even two deaths?

argumentFlow.label: Turnabout: why prepare a backup KG at all, if he's diligent?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara / Rabbanan
argumentFlow.text: The same kind of challenge is now turned back on the Rabbanan's own rule: let the Rabbanan answer for themselves - the KG is diligent enough to avoid impurity on his own, so why prepare a backup KG at all? The Rabbanan answer: it is precisely because a rival KG has been made ready that the sitting KG is spurred to be all the more diligent - the rivalry is the cause of the diligence, not a reason to dispense with the preparation.

sourceRefs.note: The Gemara asks the Rabbanan to defend their own position
Rabbanan invoke the Kohen Gadol's diligence
Challenge: if he is diligent, why appoint a backup priest?
Answer: appointing a rival makes him still more diligent; the later 'ומי סגי' clause begins the next sugya

misconceptions.misconception: R. Yehuda is being overly cautious by demanding a backup wife.
misconceptions.correction: He is applying rigorous logical symmetry: if we prepare for impurity, we must prepare for death too.

misconceptions.misconception: The Rabbanan are dismissing the risk of death as too improbable to matter.
misconceptions.correction: They are making a distinction based on frequency, not conceptual preventability - the Gemara states plainly that impurity is shechicha (common) while death is lo shechicha (not common).

misconceptions.misconception: R. Yehuda's one-death-vs-two-deaths line and the Rabbanan's rebuttal are a continuation of the original frequency distinction.
misconceptions.correction: They are a separate slippery-slope exchange: having conceded that a rare risk can matter, the Gemara asks where that concern stops, and the Rabbanan argue it should not stop at one death if it is a real concern at all.

misconceptions.misconception: The Rabbanan originally justified preparing a backup KG by his lack of diligence, or diligence is the basis of the shechicha/lo-shechicha distinction.
misconceptions.correction: Diligence appears only later, as the Rabbanan's answer to a different challenge (why prepare a backup KG if he's diligent on his own) - their answer is that the rivalry is what produces the diligence, not that diligence was ever the reason for the original frequency-based ruling.

visualizableElements.item: Tumah shechicha (impurity is common) vs. mitah lo shechicha (death is not common) - the basis for the Rabbanan's original asymmetric ruling
The six days of separation before Yom Kippur, during which impurity is a recurring, common risk, vs. a wife's death before Yom Kippur, which is a rare occurrence
R. Yehuda's one-death stopping point vs. the Rabbanan's challenge that concern should extend to two deaths
The backup KG as the cause of the sitting KG's diligence, not a redundant precaution against its absence

quizSeeds.question: Why do the Rabbanan reject R. Yehuda's call for a backup wife even though they prepare a backup KG?
quizSeeds.answer: The Gemara states the reason directly: tumah shechicha, mitah lo shechicha - impurity is a common occurrence, death is not. Preparation is warranted for the common risk, not the rare one.

sourceRefs.note: Rabbanan's objection

quizSeeds.question: What verse creates the requirement for the KG to have a wife on Yom Kippur?
quizSeeds.answer: The word 'bayto' (his house) in Leviticus 16, interpreted as requiring a wife on the day of service.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yehuda's position

quizSeeds.question: R. Yehuda is challenged that his concern for a rare risk has no stopping point. How does he limit it, and how do the Rabbanan respond?
quizSeeds.answer: R. Yehuda says he is concerned only about a single death, not a run of two deaths. The Rabbanan respond that if he is concerned at all, he should be concerned even for two deaths - his stopping point is arbitrary.

sourceRefs.note: One-death-vs-two-deaths exchange

quizSeeds.question: If the KG is expected to be diligent about avoiding impurity, why do the Rabbanan still prepare a backup KG?
quizSeeds.answer: The Rabbanan answer that the backup KG is not redundant with his diligence - it is the cause of it. Because a rival has been made ready to take his place, the sitting KG is spurred to be all the more careful.

sourceRefs.note: Rabbanan's diligence self-defense

sugyot.finalRuling: Halacha: Rabbanan - no backup wife is prepared, since the KG's wife dying before Yom Kippur is lo shechicha. A backup KG is prepared against impurity (shechicha); the Rabbanan hold that this preparation is also what spurs the sitting KG's diligence, not a measure made unnecessary by it.

display.title: Four failed conditional divorces: teaching get al tenai through an impossible case
display.oneLine: The Gemara tests four conditional divorce formulas for the KG's backup wife, and Rashi notes the section is educational, not a working solution.
display.whats: Merely designating or betrothing her doesn't work (she isn't yet his 'house' until actually married); actually marrying her creates two houses; and simply divorcing her after marrying her removes any benefit. So the Gemara tries divorcing her conditionally: (1) on condition she dies on YK - but perhaps neither wife dies, leaving him with two houses. (2) on condition she does NOT die - but perhaps she survives (valid divorce) while the original wife dies, leaving him with no wife at all. (3) on condition one of the two wives dies - but perhaps neither dies (two houses again); and even apart from that timing problem, the Gemara questions whether this formula is a valid get at all, since (per Rava) a condition tied to both spouses' own lives for as long as they live fails the Torah's keritut (complete severance) requirement. (4) on condition the other wife does NOT die - but perhaps she dies in the middle of the Yom Kippur service itself, leaving the outcome unresolved; the discussion breaks off here and continues onto 13b. Rashi notes this entire discussion is not meant to produce a working solution but to teach the logic of conditional gitin (bills of divorce).
display.hint: Why does every conditional-divorce formula fail—by leaving two wives, leaving no wife, or failing the keritut requirement—and why does the daf therefore end without a working resolution?

learning.learnerQuestion: Can any conditional divorce formula let the KG have a backup wife without ever having two wives or no wife at the moment of service?
learning.coreTension: Every formula that makes the first wife's divorce take effect at the right moment either leaves the KG with no wife at a critical point, or, if it does not take effect, leaves him with two wives.
learning.coreMove: Each of the four formulas is tested and rejected - the first three for retroactively creating a two-wife or no-wife state during the service, and the third also for failing the keritut requirement outright. Rashi concludes the section is educational, exploring the limits of get al tenai rather than producing a working solution.
learning.ahaMoment: The Torah's 'bayto' (one house) creates a logical trap: any moment the first divorce becomes valid leaves a gap; any gap risks having two houses. The puzzle is insoluble within the terms of conditional divorce law.
learning.memoryAnchor: Four doors, all locked: every conditional divorce formula either leaves the KG with two wives, no wife, or fails as a get entirely.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may expect the daf to land on a working formula since several are tried. Rashi's framing makes clear the failures are the point - they map exactly where conditional divorce law breaks down.

takeaway.text: No conditional divorce formula resolves R. Yehuda's two-wife problem. The four failed attempts map the boundaries of get al tenai rather than producing a working ruling.

argumentFlow.label: Merely designating/betrothing fails; actual marriage creates two houses
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Merely designating or betrothing a second woman doesn't help - she isn't yet his 'house' (wife) until he actually marries her. So he must actually marry her - but then he has two houses at once, which 'his house' (singular) forbids. Divorcing her again after marrying her removes any benefit, since if the first wife then dies he again has no second wife in reserve.

sourceRefs.note: Setup: why designation, betrothal, and plain marry-divorce all fail

argumentFlow.label: Formula 1: 'on condition you die on Yom Kippur'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: He marries the second wife, then gives her a get conditional on her dying on YK. If she dies, the divorce takes effect retroactively and he had only one wife; if she doesn't die but the original wife does, the second wife's marriage stands and he again has one wife. Problem: perhaps neither wife dies, leaving him with two houses on Yom Kippur.

sourceRefs.note: First conditional formula begins at Vilna line 22 within the source chunk anchored at line 20: 'al tenai she-tamuti'

argumentFlow.label: Formula 2: 'on condition you don't die'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: He gives her a get conditional on her NOT dying on YK. If she survives, she's divorced and he remains married to the original wife; if she dies, the original wife is (by assumption) still alive and he remains married to her alone. Problem: perhaps the second wife survives (so her divorce takes effect, leaving her not his wife) while the original wife dies - leaving the High Priest with no wife at all on Yom Kippur.

sourceRefs.note: Second conditional formula: 'al tenai shelo tamuti'

argumentFlow.label: Formula 3: 'on condition one of you dies' - rejected on two grounds
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: He gives her a get conditional on one of the two wives dying: if this one dies, that one is alive; if that one dies, this one is alive - seemingly covering both cases. Problem: perhaps neither dies, leaving him with two houses. And independent of that timing problem, the Gemara questions whether this is even a valid get at all: Rava ruled that a divorce conditioned on the wife not drinking wine 'all the days of my life and your life' is not a valid severance (keritut), because it keeps the parties bound to each other for as long as both live - whereas a condition tied to a third party's life (e.g., 'all the days of so-and-so's life') does count as severance. Since this formula's condition depends on the two wives' own lives rather than a third party's, it fails keritut on the same grounds.

sourceRefs.note: Third conditional formula: 'al tenai she-tamut achat mikem'
Digression: does this formula satisfy keritut? Rava's wine-condition ruling

argumentFlow.label: Formula 4: 'on condition your counterpart doesn't die' - left unresolved
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: He gives the second wife a get conditional on the first wife (her 'counterpart') not dying. If the first wife doesn't die, the second wife is divorced; if the first wife dies, the second wife remains married - seemingly covering both cases. Problem: perhaps the first wife dies in the middle of the Yom Kippur service itself, and it becomes unclear whether the second wife's divorce retroactively takes effect mid-service. The Gemara's discussion breaks off here and continues onto 13b.

sourceRefs.note: Fourth conditional formula: 'al tenai shelo tamut chavertich' - unresolved, continues on 13b

misconceptions.misconception: These conditional divorce formulas are meant to produce a practical ruling the KG could actually use.
misconceptions.correction: Rashi explicitly says they are educational examples of get al tenai logic, not a working solution.

misconceptions.misconception: The failure of all four formulas means conditional divorce is invalid generally.
misconceptions.correction: It means the specific constraints of the KG's Yom Kippur situation make resolution impossible within those rules, not that conditional divorce is unworkable elsewhere.

visualizableElements.item: Four conditional divorce formulas each rejected in turn - a chain of logical failures
The two impossible states: KG with two wives (bayto violated) vs. KG with no wife (bayto also violated)
The keritut requirement from the Torah - a get conditioned on the spouses' own lives (rather than a third party's) fails as a severance, independent of the two-wife/no-wife timing problem

quizSeeds.question: Why do all four conditional divorce formulas fail to solve the backup-wife problem?
quizSeeds.answer: The first, second, and fourth formulas each risk leaving the KG with either two wives or no wife at a critical moment, depending on who dies and when. The third formula fails for that same timing reason, and also fails independently as a valid get, since (per Rava) a condition tied to both spouses' own lives rather than a third party's life does not satisfy the Torah's keritut (severance) requirement.

sourceRefs.note: First conditional formula begins at Vilna line 22 within the source chunk anchored at line 20

quizSeeds.question: What does Rashi say about the purpose of this entire conditional-divorce section?
quizSeeds.answer: Rashi says the answers don't hold and the section is educational - teaching the rules of conditional divorce through an extreme test case, not meant to produce a working ruling.

sugyot.finalRuling: No conditional divorce formula successfully solves R. Yehuda's two-wife problem. The discussion continues on 13b.

alternateAngles.desc: This sugya is one of the Talmud's most sustained explorations of conditional divorce mechanics, using the KG's unique situation to stress-test every possible formula.

prerequisiteKnowledge: Basic rules of conditional divorce (get al tenai) in Jewish law
The keritut requirement for a valid get
R. Yehuda's backup wife position from the previous sugya

glossary.en: Rival wife in a polygamous household; used here as an analogy for the replacement KG's relationship to the original, which Rav rejects as not applicable.
Conditional bill of divorce - takes effect only if a specified condition is met. The entire second half of this daf tests four such formulas for the KG's backup-wife problem.
Complete severance - the Torah's requirement for a valid divorce (Deuteronomy 24). A formula that leaves the wife conditionally tied to the husband fails this requirement.

He is diligent - describes the KG's scrupulous attention to ritual purity. Rashi notes he guards himself from impurity, but death is not given into our hands; the Gemara's own stated ground for preparing a backup KG but not a backup wife is frequency (tumah shechicha, mitah lo shechicha), not this diligence by itself.

rashiTranslations.en: Since it says: if there is reason to be concerned, we are concerned even about the death of two - let them also say
concerning impurity: if there is reason to be concerned, we are also concerned about the impurity of two, and there is no end to the matter.
'He is diligent' - and he guards himself from impurity, but death is not given into our hands. 'through a preparation' -
through designation. 'the difficulty returns' - for perhaps she will die. 'on condition that you die' - on Yom Kippur, and if
she dies on that day, the get is found to be valid retroactively, and there is
not here except one house; and if she does not die,
and her counterpart dies, this one remains for him,
so that the get is not a get. And this entire sugya has no
resolutions within it that can fully stand, for there are
many possible answers to them, and it is only that
it teaches us the underlying point; and if you say there is
an answer of that kind, it does not address every
answer that could be given, for with one answer it removes
the difficulty by resolving it another way, until it establishes it
in its place. 'and perhaps she does not die' - and
the get is not a get. 'on condition that you do not die' - and if
she does not die, as he stated, it is a get
retroactively. 'in such a case' - that the condition is dependent
on her being alive - was it a get at all? 'this is not a severance' -
since all the days of her life she is bound to him, and we
require an actual severance. 'all the days of the life of so-and-so' -
this is a severance. And she may remarry after
so-and-so's death, and also from today it is a get,
so that if she became unfaithful there is no obligation of a married
woman here, since it is only like a concern lest she drink
wine during so-and-so's life. 'on condition your counterpart does not die' -
and if her counterpart does not die, she has a get
retroactively, and there is only one house here.
This ('if') is the catchword anticipating 13b's opening comment.
